subject: Biochemistry & genetics
summary: Molecular genetics studies how DNA sequence changes affect cell function and disease. Clinicians use it to diagnose inherited disorders, select targeted therapies, and predict prognosis.

sections.p: Molecular genetics examines the structure, function, and variation of genes at the DNA level. It links genotype to phenotype, allowing clinicians to explain disease mechanisms and personalize care.
b: DNA = genetic blueprint; mutations alter protein function.
Techniques: PCR, sequencing, microarrays, and CRISPR.

sections.p: Genes are transcribed to RNA then translated into proteins. Variants can be single‑nucleotide changes, insertions, deletions, or copy‑number alterations that disrupt this flow.
b: Missense → altered amino acid; nonsense → truncated protein.
Frameshift → downstream nonsense; splice‑site → abnormal mRNA.

sections.p: Gene expression is controlled by promoters, enhancers, epigenetic marks, and non‑coding RNAs. Dysregulation can mimic genetic defects even without DNA changes.

Pathogenic variants cause inherited diseases, predispose to cancer, or affect drug metabolism. In low‑resource settings, infections (HIV, TB, hepatitis B) can introduce viral integration or trigger mutagenesis.
b: Somatic: KRAS, EGFR mutations in lung cancer.

sections.p: Molecular tests guide diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy. They are essential for targeted cancer drugs, pharmacogenomics, and carrier screening.
b: EGFR mutation → EGFR‑TKI therapy in NSCLC.
TPMT genotype → dose adjustment for azathioprine.

t.b: Does the patient have rifampicin‑resistant TB? Positive result directs second‑line therapy.

t.a: Next‑generation sequencing panel for solid tumours
t.b: Which actionable mutations are present? Guides selection of targeted agents; if unavailable, use immunohistochemistry as surrogate.
Is the patient at risk of abacavir hypersensitivity? Positive result → avoid abacavir.

sections.p: Focus on test selection, interpretation, and therapeutic impact. Remember common tropical infections that cause secondary genetic alterations.
b: Know the main panels for leukaemia, breast, lung, and colorectal cancer.
Recall when a test is not feasible and alternative clinical criteria are used.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly progressive neurological decline with a suspected metabolic disorder.
Unexplained severe cytopenias suggesting a marrow failure syndrome.
Acute leukemia with high‑risk cytogenetics requiring urgent targeted therapy.

faq.q: Why order a genetic test if the clinical picture is clear?
faq.a: It confirms the diagnosis, informs prognosis, and may change treatment (e.g., targeted therapy).

faq.q: What if the required molecular test is unavailable?
faq.a: Use surrogate markers (immunohistochemistry, clinical criteria) and refer to a centre with the capability.

faq.q: Can infections cause false‑positive genetic results?
faq.a: Yes, viral DNA integration (e.g., HBV) can mimic somatic mutations; correlate with clinical context.

exam: Explain how EGFR mutation status influences therapy in non‑small cell lung cancer.
List three inherited metabolic disorders diagnosed by plasma amino‑acid analysis and their genetic basis.
Describe the steps and rationale for pharmacogenomic testing before starting azathioprine.
